headings.title: Introduction to Nutrition in HIV Management
headings.content: Nutrition plays a critical and foundational role in the comprehensive management of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection. For nursing students practicing in Nigeria and across sub-Saharan Africa, understanding this relationship is vital for improving patient outcomes. Good nutrition works synergistically with antiretroviral therapy (ART) to strengthen the immune system, slow the progression from HIV to AIDS, improve treatment adherence, and enhance the overall quality of life. HIV is a hypermetabolic condition that increases the body's energy expenditure while simultaneously reducing nutrient absorption due to chronic inflammation, opportunistic infections, and gastrointestinal complications. Without adequate nutritional support, patients quickly experience rapid weight loss, severe muscle wasting, and progressive immunodeficiency, which drastically increases morbidity and mortality rates. Nurses are often the primary healthcare providers on the frontline who identify early nutritional deficits during routine clinic visits. By integrating nutritional assessment and education into daily nursing care, professionals can help mitigate HIV-related wasting syndrome, reduce systemic vulnerability, and support the body's physiological capacity to tolerate complex medical regimens. Emphasizing nutrition from the time of diagnosis ensures that patients maintain optimal body composition, preserve lean tissue mass, and sustain the vital organ function necessary to withstand lifelong antiviral treatment.

headings.title: Nutritional Goals and Requirements for People Living with HIV
headings.content: Establishing specific nutritional goals and requirements for people living with HIV (PLHIV) is essential for maintaining metabolic balance and immune competence. The primary nutritional goals include maintaining or achieving a healthy body weight, preventing lean body mass loss, and correcting micronutrient deficiencies. Energy requirements for asymptomatic adults living with HIV generally increase by approximately 10 percent above the normal basal energy expenditure to account for the heightened resting metabolic rate caused by the virus. For symptomatic adults and individuals experiencing acute infections or secondary illnesses, energy requirements increase by 20 to 30 percent to support tissue healing and immune response. In the case of children living with HIV who experience growth faltering or weight loss, energy intake must be increased by 50 to 100 percent above normal recommended daily allowances to catch up on missed developmental milestones. Protein requirements must also be carefully managed to prevent muscle wasting while avoiding undue renal stress. Adequate fluid intake is equally crucial, particularly in tropical climates like Nigeria, to prevent dehydration exacerbated by common HIV-related symptoms such as chronic diarrhea, vomiting, and persistent fevers. Nurses must educate patients and caregivers on culturally accessible local food options that can successfully meet these heightened caloric and nutrient demands without placing an unsustainable financial burden on the household.

headings.title: Macronutrient and Micronutrient Management
headings.content: Macronutrient and micronutrient management forms the backbone of dietary planning for individuals managing HIV. Macronutrients—comprising carbohydrates, proteins, and healthy fats—must be balanced carefully to provide sustained energy and preserve cellular integrity. Complex carbohydrates derived from locally available sources such as yams, sweet potatoes, millet, and sorghum provide steady energy without causing sudden spikes in blood glucose. High-quality lean proteins, sourced from beans, fish, eggs, poultry, and lean meats, are vital for repairing damaged tissues and maintaining muscle mass. Healthy fats, including plant-based oils and nuts, contribute essential fatty acids and concentrated calories for individuals struggling with weight loss. Concurrently, micronutrients—vitamins and minerals—are critical because PLHIV frequently suffer from deficiencies due to poor intake, malabsorption, and increased oxidative stress. Vitamins A, C, E, and the B-complex group, alongside minerals like zinc, iron, and selenium, play indispensable roles in supporting immune cell proliferation and scavenging harmful free radicals. For instance, vitamin A supplementation in children has been shown to reduce morbidity and mortality related to measles and severe diarrheal diseases. However, nurses must advise patients against mega-dosing individual supplements without professional supervision, as excessive amounts of certain minerals can sometimes be toxic or adversely interact with antiretroviral medications, emphasizing instead a diverse, nutrient-dense diet utilizing accessible local foods.

headings.title: Nutritional Assessment and Monitoring
headings.content: Nutritional assessment and continuous monitoring are essential clinical competencies for nurses caring for patients with HIV. The assessment process typically follows the ABCDE approach: Anthropometric measurements, Biochemical data, Clinical signs, Dietary history, and Environmental factors. Anthropometric measurements, including weight, height, Body Mass Index (BMI), and Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC), help identify malnutrition, wasting, or sudden weight fluctuations. In resource-limited settings across Nigeria, MUAC tapes are especially valuable for quickly screening pregnant women and young children for acute malnutrition. Biochemical markers, such as hemoglobin levels, serum albumin, and CD4 counts, provide objective insight into anemia, systemic inflammation, and immune status. Clinical examinations involve inspecting the patient for visible signs of nutrient deficiencies, such as oral thrush, angular cheilitis, skin rashes, and muscle wasting. Taking a comprehensive dietary history reveals eating patterns, food insecurities, cultural beliefs, and barriers to adequate food access. Environmental and socioeconomic screening evaluates household food security, access to safe drinking water, and financial stability. By regularly documenting these parameters in patient charts, nurses can detect early deviations from healthy nutritional baselines, implement timely dietary interventions, and evaluate the effectiveness of ongoing nutrition support plans.

headings.title: Managing HIV-Related Symptoms and Metabolic Complications
headings.content: People living with HIV frequently experience a wide range of symptoms and metabolic complications that severely compromise dietary intake and nutritional status. Common gastrointestinal symptoms include nausea, vomiting, chronic diarrhea, dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) due to esophageal candidiasis, and loss of appetite (anorexia). Additionally, long-term antiretroviral therapy can induce metabolic complications such as dyslipidemia, insulin resistance, lipodystrophy (abnormal fat distribution), and lactic acidosis. Nurses play a pivotal role in managing these challenges through targeted non-pharmacological interventions and patient education. For patients experiencing severe nausea and vomiting, nurses should recommend eating small, frequent meals of dry, bland foods, avoiding greasy or strongly spiced dishes, and consuming fluids between meals rather than during them to prevent gastric distension. For oral thrush or painful swallowing, advising soft, pureed, or room-temperature foods can prevent further irritation. When managing chronic diarrhea, nurses must emphasize adequate hydration with oral rehydration salts (ORS) and safe fluids, alongside low-fiber binding foods like bananas, rice, and boiled potatoes. For metabolic complications like dyslipidemia, nurses should counsel patients on reducing saturated fats and increasing physical activity, working collaboratively with physicians and dietitians to optimize overall health outcomes.

headings.title: Drug-Nutrient Interactions in Antiretroviral Therapy
headings.content: Drug-nutrient interactions represent a critical intersection of pharmacology and nutrition in HIV management. Antiretroviral drugs can significantly alter nutrient absorption, metabolism, and excretion, while conversely, certain foods can affect the bioavailability and therapeutic efficacy of medications. For example, some protease inhibitors and non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors require specific dietary conditions, such as being taken with a high-fat meal, to ensure optimal absorption into the bloodstream. On the other hand, certain medications may cause severe gastrointestinal upset if taken on an empty stomach, or conversely, must be taken fasting to avoid food binding that renders the drug inactive. Furthermore, chronic use of specific antiretrovirals can lead to micronutrient depletions, bone mineral density loss, and alterations in lipid profiles. Herbal supplements and traditional remedies frequently used alongside conventional medicine in Nigeria must also be evaluated carefully by nurses, as substances like St. John's Wort can drastically reduce antiretroviral drug levels through hepatic enzyme induction, leading to treatment failure and viral resistance. Nurses must conduct thorough medication histories, educate patients on precise timing regarding meals and drug administration, and emphasize adherence to specific dietary instructions provided by the multidisciplinary healthcare team.

headings.title: Food Safety, Hygiene, and Water Sanitation
headings.content: Food safety, personal hygiene, and water sanitation are paramount in HIV management because compromised immunity leaves individuals exceptionally vulnerable to foodborne and waterborne pathogens. Microorganisms such as Salmonella, Cryptosporidium, Toxoplasma, and Listeria, which might cause mild illness in healthy individuals, can trigger severe, life-threatening gastroenteritis, systemic infections, and chronic diarrhea in people living with HIV. Nurses must educate patients and their families on rigorous hygiene practices, including thorough handwashing with soap and clean water before preparing, serving, and eating food, as well as after using the toilet or handling raw meats. Food preparation practices must emphasize cooking meats, poultry, and eggs thoroughly to destroy harmful bacteria and parasites, avoiding unpasteurized dairy products, and washing all raw fruits and vegetables extensively with clean, safe water. In settings where tap water safety is uncertain, boiling water for drinking and food preparation or utilizing appropriate household water treatment methods is vital. Furthermore, leftover foods should be stored properly and reheated thoroughly before consumption, and cross-contamination between raw and cooked foods must be actively prevented in the kitchen. Empowering patients with these practical sanitation skills significantly reduces hospital admissions and enhances overall health stability.

headings.title: Counseling and Support Strategies for Nurses
headings.content: Counseling and support strategies are central to effective nursing care in HIV nutrition management, bridging the gap between clinical recommendations and sustainable lifestyle changes. Nutritional counseling must be tailored, empathetic, and culturally sensitive, respecting local dietary habits, economic constraints, and food availability within Nigerian communities. Nurses should utilize a patient-centered approach, actively listening to clients' barriers regarding food access, stigma, and physical symptoms while providing practical, affordable solutions. Establishing peer support groups can also empower patients by creating a safe space to share experiences, recipes, and coping mechanisms for managing side effects and food insecurity. Furthermore, nurses should facilitate linkages to community-based organizations, social welfare programs, and agricultural initiatives that provide nutritional aid or livelihood support for vulnerable households. Effective counseling goes beyond mere instruction; it involves building trust, assessing readiness to change, and offering continuous encouragement. By fostering a supportive therapeutic relationship, nurses help patients overcome psychological hurdles associated with chronic illness, bolster adherence to dietary and medical regimens, and promote long-term health and well-being.
